geometry.label: Room Length
geometry.rationale: Floor plan area is a primary determinant of perceived spaciousness. Longer rooms alter sightlines, furniture arrangement options, and sense of freedom versus confinement.

geometry.label: Room Width
geometry.rationale: Width relative to length controls the aspect ratio and degree of perceived enclosure. Narrow rooms increase enclosure; wider rooms increase perceived openness.

geometry.label: Ceiling Height
geometry.rationale: Higher ceilings prime abstract, expansive thinking; lower ceilings prime concrete, detail-focused thinking. The 2.0–3.5 m range spans below-standard to high-end residential. Default 2.7 m approximates the empirical preference peak reported by Vartanian et al.

windows.label: Number of Windows
windows.construct: daylight access / view quality / restorative potential
windows.rationale: Window count affects both the total daylight admitted and the number of view opportunities. Views of the exterior—particularly nature—support attention restoration and stress reduction.

windows.label: Window-to-Wall Ratio
windows.rationale: Glazing ratio is the primary architectural determinant of daylight factor. It interacts with daylight_intensity to determine the absolute illumination level reaching occupants.

windows.label: Window Sill Height
windows.rationale: Sill height determines whether occupants can see the exterior while seated. Lower sills provide unobstructed seated views; higher sills restrict views to standing occupants.

windows.label: Window Treatment
windows.construct: daylight modulation / privacy / thermal comfort perception
windows.rationale: Window coverings modulate admitted daylight and signal privacy level. Sheer curtains diffuse glare while maintaining view. Heavy curtains increase enclosure and reduce stimulation. The choice also acts as a material warmth cue.

windows.label: Exterior View Type
windows.rationale: The content of a window view—independent of window size—is a strong predictor of stress recovery and attention restoration. Nature views consistently outperform built or obstructed views.

doors.label: Number of Doors
doors.rationale: Door count and placement affect perceived connectivity between spaces, sense of privacy, and feeling of potential escape or openness—relevant to feelings of control and safety.

doors.label: Door Style
doors.rationale: Door style contributes to perceived formality and material richness of the interior. Glass-panel doors introduce borrowed light and visual connectivity; flush doors recede into walls.

lighting.label: Daylight Intensity
lighting.rationale: Daylight exposure affects alertness, mood, restoration, and circadian regulation. Brighter daylight environments are associated with higher positive affect and improved cognitive performance in office and residential studies.
lighting.citation: Kaplan & Kaplan (1989); Münch et al. (2020); Heschong (1999)

lighting.label: Artificial Light Intensity
lighting.rationale: Artificial lighting supplements daylight and is the primary light source in evening conditions. Higher intensity artificial light increases arousal and perceived energy level; lower intensity creates a more intimate atmosphere.

lighting.label: Light Color Temperature
lighting.rationale: Warm light (2700–3000 K) is associated with relaxation, lower arousal, and evening-appropriate environments. Cool light (5000–6500 K) increases alertness, accuracy, and corresponds to midday daylight. This parameter controls the spectral character of both artificial and ambient sky colour.
lighting.citation: Knez (1995); Küller et al. (2006); van Duijnhoven et al. (2017)

lighting.label: Primary Light Source Type
lighting.construct: light distribution / perceived intimacy / vertical illumination ratio
lighting.rationale: Light source type determines the distribution and directionality of illumination. Overhead lighting produces flat, even light; floor and table lamps create pools of warm light associated with intimacy and reduced visual fatigue.

lighting.label: Shadow Softness
lighting.rationale: Sharp shadows (low value) suggest direct, high-altitude sunlight or hard artificial sources. Soft shadows suggest diffuse overcast sky or softbox-style sources. Shadow character is a strong cue for perceived time of day and light quality.

materials.label: Wall Colour Hue
materials.rationale: Hue is the strongest driver of colour-related emotional response. Blues and greens are associated with calm and restoration; yellows and reds with warmth and arousal. The full hue circle is exposed to support a wide range of experimental manipulations. Default 30° is a warm neutral (off-white/cream).
materials.citation: Kaya & Epps (2004); Valdez & Mehrabian (1994); Küller et al. (2006)

materials.label: Wall Colour Saturation
materials.rationale: Higher saturation amplifies the arousal potential of any hue. Highly saturated residential walls are unusual and visually fatiguing over extended exposure; desaturated walls are typical of calming residential interiors. Default 0.08 reflects common practice.

materials.label: Wall Colour Lightness
materials.rationale: Lighter walls reflect more light, increase perceived brightness and spaciousness, and lower perceived enclosure. Dark walls reduce perceived room volume. This parameter interacts with daylight_intensity.

materials.label: Floor Material
materials.construct: warmth perception / acoustic comfort / formality / cleanliness perception
materials.rationale: Floor material is a dominant surface in any room and strongly shapes warmth, formality, and perceived hygiene. Carpet signals softness and acoustic comfort; hardwood signals formality and cleanliness; tile signals hard, cool surfaces.

materials.label: Ceiling Material
materials.rationale: Ceiling material affects perceived height through reflectance (smooth white maximises perceived height) and adds visual complexity. Exposed wood panels are associated with warmth and natural materials.

furniture.label: Furniture Density
furniture.rationale: Furniture density is a proxy for the visual and navigational clutter of a room. Higher density increases perceived crowding and cognitive load; lower density increases perceived spaciousness but may signal emptiness or lack of comfort.

furniture.label: Seating Count
furniture.rationale: The number of seats signals the intended social scale of a room—intimate (2–3) versus group/party (6–8). This affects perceived social affordance, privacy, and territorial density.

furniture.label: Furniture Arrangement
furniture.construct: social facilitation / attentional focus / territorial organisation
furniture.rationale: Furniture arrangement determines whether the room primes face-to-face social interaction (conversational), media consumption (parallel_tv_facing), individual activity (dispersed), or a hybrid (l_shape). This is a primary determinant of social behaviour in experimental settings.

furniture.label: Sofa Style
furniture.rationale: Sofa style is the dominant furniture object in a living room and communicates both aesthetic register (modern vs. traditional) and comfort affordance. Low modern sofas signal informality; upright traditional sofas signal formality.

furniture.label: Coffee Table Present
furniture.rationale: A coffee table anchors the seating arrangement and defines a proxemic centre. Its presence implies a more formalised social zone; its absence suggests a more open or casual space.

furniture.label: Bookshelf Present
furniture.construct: identity signalling / intellectual cue / visual complexity
furniture.rationale: Bookshelves are a recognised marker of intellectual identity and openness to experience. Their presence changes inferences about the room's occupants and adds structured visual complexity.

furniture.label: Television Present
furniture.construct: attentional focus / media affordance / furniture arrangement anchor
furniture.rationale: A television is a dominant focal object in most living rooms and reshapes furniture arrangement, attentional direction, and the perceived primary activity of the space.

furniture.label: Clutter Level
furniture.construct: cognitive load / chronic stress / restoration inhibition
furniture.rationale: Household clutter is associated with elevated cortisol, reduced restoration, and impaired attentional recovery. This parameter controls the overall disorder of surfaces, floors, and furniture.

plants.label: Plant Count
plants.construct: biophilic connection / attention restoration / stress reduction
plants.rationale: Indoor plants are a core biophilic design element. Exposure to indoor vegetation reduces physiological stress markers and supports attentional restoration. Even a single plant measurably shifts the biophilic character of a scene.

plants.label: Plant Size
plants.construct: biophilic visual salience / spatial volume occupied
plants.rationale: Larger plants command more visual attention and occupy more volume, increasing the biophilic signal strength of the room. Floor-standing plants also serve as spatial dividers.

plants.label: Plant Species Type
plants.rationale: Plant form affects the character of biophilic exposure. Tropical leafy plants provide high organic complexity and fractal-like form associated with attention restoration. Succulent geometric forms are lower complexity. Flowering plants add colour stimulation.
plants.citation: Joye (2007); Taylor et al. (2005) — fractal dimension of nature

decoration.label: Painting / Art Count
decoration.construct: visual complexity / aesthetic preference / identity signalling
decoration.rationale: Wall art contributes to visual complexity and signals personality traits of the room's occupant. Multiple pieces increase overall visual complexity and provide focal objects for attentional dwell.

decoration.label: Painting Style
decoration.construct: restorative potential / aesthetic preference / content-specific affect
decoration.rationale: Painting content has independent effects from painting quantity. Nature landscapes support restoration (Attention Restoration Theory). Abstract geometric art increases perceived modernity. Figurative portraits introduce social presence cues.

decoration.label: Painting Size
decoration.rationale: Large statement artworks function as architectural focal elements and dominate attentional capture. Smaller pieces are contextual. This interacts with painting_count to determine total wall art complexity.

decoration.label: Decoration Density
decoration.rationale: Berlyne's complexity–preference framework predicts an inverted-U relationship between visual complexity and aesthetic preference. Moderate decoration density is preferred; very low density reads as bare and cold; very high density reads as chaotic.

decoration.label: Rug Present
decoration.construct: zone definition / warmth cue / acoustic softness signal
decoration.rationale: A rug anchors the seating zone visually, adds a warmth and softness cue independent of floor material, and signals acoustic comfort (sound dampening). Its presence or absence visibly changes the spatial organisation of the room.

decoration.label: Object Arrangement Order
decoration.rationale: The orderliness of surfaces and objects is a driver of stress and perceived control. A cluttered, disordered environment impairs restoration; a neat environment signals control and organisation.

decoration.label: Mirror Present
decoration.rationale: Mirrors increase perceived room depth and spaciousness. They also increase self-focused attention, which can modulate social behaviour and self-evaluation in experimental contexts.
